title: Chukat: Miriam's well (Numbers 20:1–2)
hook: Miriam dies and the water stops; the Talmud says a well went with them for her sake (Taanit 9a)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the red heifer: ashes that cleanse one person and make another impure, a chok with no stated reason. Your line was not everything explains itself. Did you let one thing stay unexplained? Day four hundred fifty-seven.

Some people hold a family together so quietly that nobody notices until they're gone. The grandmother whose kitchen was where everyone ended up. The coworker who refilled the coffee and remembered birthdays. After the funeral, something stops working, and only then does everyone realize who was doing it. The Torah has a verse like that. In one short line, Miriam, the sister of Moses and Aaron, dies and is buried. And in the very next line, there's no water.
screen: `THE ONE WHO HELD IT TOGETHER.` → `MIRIAM DIES.` → `THEN THERE'S NO WATER.`

segments.voice: The Torah's words are spare. In paraphrase: the people came to the wilderness of Zin and stayed at Kadesh, and Miriam died there and was buried there. Then: there was no water for the congregation. That's all. No weeping is recorded for her, no days of mourning, nothing like what the Torah will record for Aaron and later for Moses. But the rabbis read the two verses together and heard something. In the Talmud, tractate Taanit, Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Yehuda teaches that three good leaders rose up for Israel: Moses, Aaron and Miriam. And three good gifts came through them: the manna, for Moses' sake; the clouds of glory, for Aaron's sake; and the well, for Miriam's sake. A well of water traveled with the people through the desert, the rabbis say, because of her. When she died, the well went dry, and that's why the very next verse says there was no water. Why Miriam and water? Look at her story. As a girl, tradition says, she was the sister who stood by the Nile, watching her baby brother float in a basket among the reeds. At the Sea, she took a timbrel and led the women in song after they crossed the water. Water follows her all the way through. The Torah never mentions a well; this is the rabbis reading between two verses. But the picture has stayed. Today some families set a cup of water for Miriam on their Passover table. The well was her quiet gift. Nobody named it while it flowed.
screen: `SHE DIED; THERE WAS NO WATER.` · `THREE LEADERS, THREE GIFTS.` · `THE WELL, FOR MIRIAM'S SAKE.` · `WATER ALL THROUGH HER STORY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank someone who quietly sustained you. Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself: who has been a well in my life? Someone who kept things flowing without asking for credit. A parent, a teacher, a neighbor, a friend who always checked in. Picture them clearly. If they're living, decide how you'll thank them this week, in a message, a call, a note. If they've died, simply hold their name for a few breaths, and say it quietly if you'd like. Breathe until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Chukat. The portion where Miriam dies, the water stops, and the rabbis hear a well that had followed her all along.
Your line: miriam's well. Today, notice one thing that works only because someone quietly keeps it working, and tell them you noticed. Day four hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Miriam's death is read in synagogue as part of the portion of Chukat; today some families place a cup of water for Miriam, called Miriam's cup, on the Passover seder table.

match.prompt: three leaders, three gifts — tap the pairs.

myth: the Torah describes Miriam's well in detail
the Torah never mentions a well. the rabbis read it from two verses: Miriam died, then there was no water.
the Torah describes the people mourning Miriam
it records only that she died and was buried. no mourning is described.
Miriam led the women in song at the Sea
she took a timbrel and the women followed her, singing (Exodus 15:20–21).

fork.setup: you're a rabbi reading Numbers 20. Miriam dies in verse one, and in verse two there's no water. what do you make of it?
options: the water came because of her, and left with her.
fork.reveal: the Talmud reads it as a well that traveled with Israel for Miriam's sake, and stopped when she died.

original.note: Hebrew: Miriam's well, the rabbis' name for the water that followed Israel for her sake.

trapdoor: what you thought: a well named after Moses' sister.
what it means: the rabbis' reading that water followed the people through the desert because of Miriam, and stopped when she died.
what a scholar hears: Taanit 9a builds it from the juxtaposition of Numbers 20:1 and 20:2, giving each of the three siblings a gift: manna, clouds, well.

notes: Taanit 9a: Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Yehuda; three providers (Moses, Aaron, Miriam), three gifts (manna, clouds of glory, well); well departs at Miriam's death and returns in the merit of Moses and Aaron. Confirm attribution.
Exodus 2:4 does not name the sister who watched; tradition identifies her as Miriam. A Keeper may want this said explicitly.
Miriam's cup is a modern custom (late twentieth century); confirm framing.
The observation that no mourning is recorded for Miriam is from the plain text; confirm.
